ZURICH, Oct 20 : ABB is continuing to see a boom in spending on data centres used to power artificial intelligence, the engineering group said on Tuesday, as it reported its latest earnings. The Swiss company said its operational earnings before interest, tax and amortisation jumped 24 per cent to $2.03 billion in the three months to the end of September, slightly ahead of analyst forecasts for $2.0 billion. Revenue meanwhile rose 14 per cent to $9.70 billion, slightly below forecasts of $9.74 billion in a company gathered consensus. ABB, which makes electrification and automation products used by factories, ships and ports, has been seeing strong demand for products like power distribution and cooling systems used in data centres. A surge in spending on AI and data centres is propping up the global economy, helping it withstand the energy shock from the Middle East war, the IMF said last week, although it said a reassessment of efficiency gains from adopting the technology could dent investment. During the third quarter ABB said it had seen a triple digit increase in orders for data centre products, continuing the trend it saw during the second quarter.

Source: Reuters

Oct 20 : French cloud operator OVHcloud said on Tuesday its revenue rose 7.2 per cent to €1.15 billion ($1.29 billion) in the year to August 31, and that it posted its first positive levered free cash flow since its 2021 listing.  The milestone means the French group now covers its heavy capital spending from its own operations, after five years of losses on cash generation since the listing. It also forecast growth above 10 per cent for fiscal 2027, up from 7.2 per cent this year. • Levered free cash flow reached €24.7 million, against a negative €27.0 million a year earlier. • Adjusted EBITDA rose 9.7 per cent to €480.5 million, a margin of 42.0 per cent, while Public cloud revenue rose 18.9 per cent to €255.1 million.

FAST

SINGAPORE: Singapore-headquartered tech conglomerate Sea Limited is planning a public listing for its financial services arm Monee and will also launch an AI enterprise platform business, according to an internal memo sent on Tuesday (Oct 20). Founder Forrest Li, in a memo to employees that was reviewed by Reuters, said he believed going public would give its financial payments and services business the "resources and the room to go further and faster than it can today”.  The business operates in Singapore, Indonesia, Malaysia, Thailand, Vietnam, the Philippines, Taiwan, and Brazil and offers mobile wallets, payments processing, credit and banking services. Sea did not immediately respond to a request for comment. The memo said the tech group would also launch an AI-first enterprise platform named Sea Cloud.  In the memo, which was sent on the ninth anniversary of the group’s public listing in New York, Li said the quarterly revenue for the group had grown more than 80 times over that period to US$7.8 billion.

Oct 20 : Stephen Fleming is the fifth foreign coach to take charge of England's test team but the New Zealander hopes his successors will be English and says he will seek to develop home-grown coaching talent during his tenure. Fleming was appointed in July to replace compatriot Brendon McCullum, with Australian Trevor Bayliss and Zimbabwe's Duncan Fletcher and Andy Flower the other foreign coaches to have been at the helm of the test side. "I do believe that primarily the national team should be coached by a national representative," Fleming told the BBC in a podcast released on Monday. "I'm grateful for the opportunity, but there will be some development in terms of the coaching, and you can see by our staff," added the 53-year-old, who named former England players Marcus Trescothick, Richard Dawson and James Foster among his backroom staff last week.

SYDNEY: Australian barber Ricky Jefferies has been hailed as a hero for running out of his store to detain a man who authorities allege deliberately drove a car into lawmaker Helen Haines in the small town of Wangaratta, an incident that has shocked the country.    Jefferies had just finished haircuts for a young family on Monday (Oct 19) when he said he heard a "loud bang" outside his shop and realised the driver of a Toyota LandCruiser had struck Haines, leaving her badly injured. "It was crazy, I just ran out the front to see what was happening," he told reporters on Tuesday. He said he ran to assist the well-respected local MP, grabbing a knife from the alleged attacker's pocket and pulling him out of the car.

"He did have a knife. He didn't pull it out. I just wasn't comfortable with his movements, and so I basically just took it out of his pocket and threw it away," he said. Jefferies said he then held the man down until police arrived. "I just leant over him and once he was on the ground and he was no longer a threat, I just stood with him and I told him that he can't leave," he said.

Members of the police stand guard at the crime scene of a vehicle attack on Australian lawmaker Helen Haines in Wangaratta, Australia on Oct 19, 2026 in this screen grab obtained from a video. (Photo: Australian Broadcasting Corporation via Reuters)

Haines, 65, was airlifted to hospital where she underwent surgery overnight. She remains in a critical condition.  Early investigations suggested the driver, identified as a 43-year-old man, performed a U-turn before hitting Haines as she was loading or unloading things from the trunk of her car, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said . Counterterrorism authorities are among the multiple agencies involved in the investigation. While police have given no motive for the alleged attack, the involvement of counterterrorism investigators has raised alarm that it could have been an act of political violence, which is rare in Australia. Jefferies, whose shop is next door to Haines' electorate office around three hours' drive northeast of Melbourne, described the former midwife as a "genuine, kind person". Albanese praised Jefferies' intervention, calling him a hero. "At this dark and terrible time, an element of light is the fact that a Good Samaritan, someone rushed to Helen's defence in Wangaratta, put themselves potentially at risk by doing so. And that person is a hero today," Albanese said in an interview with the Nine network's "Today" show.  Jefferies downplayed the praise. "I don't think I'm a hero. I think that I just was a person who had an opportunity to intervene in a safe-ish sort of way," he said.

FAST

LONDON, Oct 20 : Demand for safe-haven assets is strong as AI jitters hurt tech stocks, the Iran war continues and keeps energy prices elevated, while worries about high government debt loads persist. Yet traditional safe havens have not performed as well as expected this year: Gold sold off after the start of the Iran war as investors ditched top-performing assets given losses elsewhere. Government bonds, once considered one of the world's safest assets, are volatile. Here is a look at how some safe havens currently stack up. 1) LOVE/HATE RELATIONSHIP WITH THE DOLLAR

Breaking with last year's 'sell US' theme, the dollar has rallied since the Iran war started, up 4 per cent since late February. That has reinforced its role as a go-to safe haven at times of global stress. A strong economy, higher rates, and the US's energy-exporter status have helped. But factors that caused traders to question the dollar's long-term safe-haven status, such as a more than $40 trillion debt pile and policy uncertainty, have not dissipated. The dollar is also vulnerable to tech selling as it has benefited from record capital inflows into US shares on optimism over the AI investment boom. The dollar could be nearing the back end of a bull market, Societe Generale chief FX strategist Kit Juckes said. "It hasn't got that much further to go," he noted, but said it was hard to justify a sustained bet against the dollar at present because the "big global story is that the dollar is a petrocurrency and we're in the middle of an energy crisis". 2) EUROPE WOBBLES, BUY SWISSIE One takeaway from France-driven bond turmoil is that the Swiss franc is a haven of choice when Europe wobbles. It is up over 2 per cent so far this month against the euro, poised for its biggest monthly jump since late 2023. "Concerns about France's public finances and election uncertainty in France and Spain have supported the franc," said Georgette Boele, senior FX & oil strategist at ABN Amro. She added that investors were also becoming less keen to use the franc to fund carry trades, preferring not to position against a currency with safe-haven qualities. Swiss rates at 0 per cent make the franc popular in trades where investors borrow in a currency with low rates to invest in higher-yielding assets elsewhere. The AI jitters should also benefit the Swiss franc, analysts said. 3) GERMAN BONDS A RELATIVE WINNER Government bonds' reputation as a safe haven has been battered by fiscal concerns. Borrowing costs from the US to Japan recently hit multi-decade highs. The tech-driven stocks selloff has, however, renewed some demand for bonds. There is another noticeable development. When US and French 10-year bond yields hit 24-year peaks earlier this month, German yields fell as their prices rose. Investors say that is a clear sign that triple-A rated German Bunds stand out as safe havens among major economies. Bundesbank President Joachim Nagel said Germany would remain the anchor of stability in Europe amid bond turmoil and was "getting fit" after years of stagnation. "Everyone worries about contagion in Europe and whether the Bund just gets dragged along with (French) OATs, (Italian) BTPs, so it's good that the Bund has acted as that European risk-off instrument," said Johnathan Owen, a portfolio manager at TwentyFour Asset Management. 4) DID YOU FORGET SHORT-DATED BONDS? Overall, high debt among major economies will continue to hurt long-dated bonds' safe-haven status, investors said. But short-dated government bonds provide some shelter because they are less sensitive to debt worries. "We really like short-dated bonds," said Rory McPherson, chief market strategist at Wren Sterling. "Because of all the concerns over debts and deficits, we haven't been buying longer-dated bonds." 5) GOLD KEEPS ITS SPARKLE Gold, another traditional safe haven, has had a bumpy ride. After hitting record highs at $5,595 per troy ounce in January, it fell after the Iran war started as investors tapped the precious metal, given losses elsewhere. Gold rallied again in August as inflation fears and concern that the Federal Reserve was not doing enough to contain price pressures returned. It is trading around $4,175. Central bank buying and safe-haven demand support prices above $4,000, analysts say. While high interest rates should limit gold's upside, a tense geopolitical backdrop and US fiscal worries should bolster the safe-haven metal further out. "In the longer term, gold should again benefit from continued strong central-bank buying and renewed concerns over US debt and its rising interest burden," said Julius Baer analyst Carsten Menke.

Source: Reuters

SEOUL: South Korea on Tuesday (Oct 20) vowed a stern response if North Korea acts on threats to strengthen its military posture along the border, which have   tensions on the Korean Peninsula. In a statement, Seoul's Defence Ministry expressed grave concern over Pyongyang's threats to deploy additional tactical strike weapons along the border and resume loudspeaker broadcasts towards the South. The escalation and exchange of threats has raised the possibility of clashes along the heavily armed border and undercuts diplomatic gains made by South Korean President Lee Jae Myung soon after he took office.  The ministry said South Korea's broadcasts and warning shots near the Military Demarcation Line (MDL) were a "legitimate defensive measure" aimed at preventing incursions and forcing North Korean troops who crossed the line to withdraw.

"If North Korea uses our legitimate measures as a pretext to carry out further provocations, we will punish it resolutely,” the ministry said. It urged Pyongyang to stop making what it called groundless claims, halt incursions across the MDL and respond to efforts to resolve differences between the two sides over the line. "CLEAR PROVOCATION" Seoul's Joint Chiefs of Staff Chairman Jin Young-seung reviewed military readiness while visiting a frontline army command, and ordered operations aimed at strengthening Seoul’s initiative in the Demilitarised Zone, its military said in a separate statement. "We cannot tolerate North Korea falsely characterising our legitimate operational measures as provocations and shifting responsibility for heightened military tensions onto our military,” Jin said. He said North Korea was responsible for planting landmines south of the MDL that seriously wounded South Korean soldiers last month, calling the incident “a clear provocation” and a violation of the armistice agreement.

The warnings from Seoul came after North Korea’s Kim Yo Jong, sister of leader Kim Jong Un, accused the South Korean military of endangering North Korean soldiers by firing warning shots during Pyongyang’s work to fortify the border. Her threat to revive North Korean loudspeaker broadcasts risks reversing a key de-escalation measure that Lee has touted as an early achievement of his efforts to restart diplomacy with Pyongyang. North Korea has been installing mines and barriers along the border since April 2024. South Korea said this month that Pyongyang had deployed as many as 7,000 workers to the area this year and that North Korean personnel had crossed the MDL on about 50 occasions. Analysts said the standoff increased the risk of a military clash. "If North Korea’s threshold falls below South Korea’s existing rules of engagement, the simple repetition of current procedures could be enough to create the conditions for a clash,” said Hong Min, a senior research fellow at the Korea Institute for National Unification. Michael Bosack, founding director of the Parley Policy Institute and a former UN Command official, said troops could mistake warning shots for missed attacks, risking “misinterpretation of intent and potential counterfires”.
